info.title: Neutrino CoreAPI
info.description:
The HTTP API of a Neutrino set-top box: channels and the guide, timers and recordings, the screen and the remote control, settings, storage and the box itself. This document is built by the box from the route tables it serves, so it always matches this build.

**Access.** Each operation states the level it needs in `x-auth-level`: `public`, `read`, `write` or `system`. A caller on a network the server trusts for reading (`lan_read`, by default the loopback addresses and the private address ranges) gets `read` without credentials, unless `nhttpd-access.conf` has a `trusted_proxies` line, even an empty one; then nobody does. Callers elsewhere, and anything beyond `read`, need a session from `POST /api/v1/login` (a cookie, plus the `X-CSRF-Token` header on every request that changes something) or a bearer token of level `read`, `write` or `system` from `api_tokens` in `nhttpd-access.conf`. `GET /api/v1/session` says what the current request is granted.

While the box still uses a password it shipped with, or a first password it made up for itself, it holds back every caller that may write: a session or a `system` token reaches only `POST /api/v1/login`, `GET /api/v1/session`, `POST /api/v1/logout` and `PUT /api/v1/account/password`, and a `write` token only the first three. Every other operation it could use refuses it with `403 password-change-required` until a password of the owner's own is set. Reading from a trusted network without credentials, or with a `read` token, is not affected.

**Values.** Channel, event and guide ids are hexadecimal strings of up to 16 digits. Moments are Unix time in seconds (UTC); durations state their unit. Request bodies are JSON objects; members a route does not declare are refused.

**Refusals** are `application/problem+json` objects whose `type` ends in a stable code such as `box-in-standby`; each operation lists its own codes with an example. The exceptions are three refusals the web server sends before a request reaches the API: `400` for a request it cannot read, `408` for a body that does not arrive in time and `501` for a method it does not take. They come as a status line and headers, with no body.

**Changes** made by any client, or on the box itself, are announced on the event stream `GET /api/v1/events`, so a client can follow the box without polling.

tags.name: auth
tags.description: Opening a session, saying what the request carries, and closing it. Everything that changes this box wants one of these first, and a caller that skips them meets a refusal rather than an answer.

tags.name: channels
tags.description: What this box can tune to and what it is tuned to now, the bouquets that group and order them, the logos beside them, and switching over.

tags.name: epg
tags.description: The guide: what is on now, what is on one channel later, a window across several channels at once, a search over all of it, and what an outside guide file contributed.

tags.name: timers
tags.description: What this box has been told to do later, and the records that say so: record, switch over, stand by, and wake.

tags.name: recordings
tags.description: What is being recorded at this moment, timeshift included, and stopping one of them.

tags.name: playback
tags.description: What the television shows: a live channel, a recording or another file, and where the player stands in it.

tags.name: osd
tags.description: The screen somebody is sitting in front of: the message on it, the volume, the keys a remote sends, and a picture of what it shows.

tags.name: settings
tags.description: The box's own settings, as the sections they are kept in, the rows each section declares, and the shape a caller has to send to change one.

tags.name: system
tags.description: What this box is and how it is doing: its build, its load, its time, the programs it runs, standby, and the 3 calls that reboot it, switch it off or restart its program.

tags.name: webserver
tags.description: The server answering this request, as it is set up: the port and the address it listens on, the one account it takes a password under, who reads from it without presenting one, and whether it hands channel pictures over. The only part of this box that can cut the way it is being changed through.

tags.name: webui
tags.description: What the web interface keeps of its own beside the box's settings: the start page, the box's name and colour as the pages show them, the devices it wakes, and which extensions it shows.

tags.name: network
tags.description: What the box does on its network for somebody else: waking a device that sleeps.

tags.name: daemons
tags.description: Starting, stopping and restarting one of the programs beside the one answering here. What they are and how they are doing is under system.

tags.name: storage
tags.description: The places this box writes to and the files on them: the mounts it knows, a directory, and one file read or written whole.

tags.name: netfs
tags.description: The filesystems this box mounts from another machine, as the 8 entries each of its 2 tables holds rather than as the lines of a file: the ones mounted at start up and kept, and the ones the automounter brings up when somebody looks at them. Passwords go in and never come back out.

tags.name: tuner
tags.description: The tuners this hardware has, what each of them is doing, the signal it is seeing, and putting them down and up again for a picture that has gone.

tags.name: plugins
tags.description: The plugins installed on this box and starting one of them.

tags.name: stream
tags.description: Live television and radio off this box's tuners: the address and the playlists a player opens on the box's own streaming port, and a channel as a browser plays it, the picture copied and the sound converted where a browser cannot decode it.

tags.name: webtv
tags.description: The channels this box plays from an address somewhere else rather than off an aerial, fetched here and handed on under this box's own name, so that a browser talks to one server instead of 2. No route here takes an address: it takes a channel of this box, or a name this box minted for an address it read out of that channel's playlist.

tags.name: config
tags.description: The box's configuration documents as whole files, read as they are on disk, and telling the program to read its configuration again. Not the settings above: these are the files underneath them, and nothing here checks what is put in one.

tags.name: events
tags.description: The one stream a client stays connected to, to be told what changed instead of asking again.

tags.name: openapi
tags.description: This document, as the box builds it out of the tables above rather than out of anything written by hand, and the one route that hands it over.

type.description: the kind of refusal, as a path ending in the refusal code (e.g. `box-in-standby`); branch on that code, not on `title` or `detail`

title.description: the name of the HTTP status the answer was sent with, for people (e.g. `Forbidden`); one refusal code can come with different titles, so branch on the code in `type`

status.description: the HTTP status this answer was sent with, repeated in the body

detail.description: what was found wrong, which is the one member here that quotes what the caller sent

depends_on.description: present only for `setting-condition-not-met`, with the keys of the settings whose values refused this one, which `detail` names as well, and for `no-free-tuner` where switching the TV picture would free a tuner, with the key of the setting that allows a stream to do that; the answer repeats the keys in the header `X-Depends-On`, separated by commas, so the answer to a HEAD names them too

get.summary: the channels the box holds, a page at a time
get.description:
Lists the channels of the television or the radio list, or of 1 bouquet, a page at a time, a whole list by the number the box shows beside each channel and a bouquet in its own order. Each entry carries the channel `id` that every other route takes.

To read the whole list, send the first request without `cursor`, then repeat with `cursor` set to the `next_cursor` of the answer until an answer has no `next_cursor`. The cursor is a channel id, not an offset, so the pages keep their place while the list keeps its order; a reload that reorders the list between 2 pages can repeat or leave out channels, so start again without `cursor` once the list changed. A channel listed twice in a bouquet is answered once.

**Refusals:**
- `400 no-such-channel`: `cursor` names a channel this list does not hold, for example after the list changed; start again without `cursor`.
- `404 no-such-bouquet`: no bouquet has that `bouquet` number; read the numbers from `GET /api/v1/bouquets`.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/channels/{id}` for 1 channel with its streams, `GET /api/v1/bouquets`, `POST /api/v1/zap`.

- `radio`: the radio list, which radio and web radio channels are in

**Preconditions:** the box is not in standby and plays a channel, not a recording or a file.

**Refusals:**

post.summary: makes a bouquet with nothing in it
post.description:
Makes a new, empty user bouquet. Fill it with `PUT /api/v1/bouquets/{bouquet}/channels`. The answer is `201` once the box has written its bouquet file and the new name reads back from its list; no `Location` header, the bouquet is addressed by the name that was sent.

**Side effects:** the bouquet files are written, and every client sees a `bouquets-changed` event on `GET /api/v1/events`.

**Refusals:**
- `409 name-taken`: a bouquet of that name exists; choose another name.
- `500 bouquet-not-changed`: the box did not take the change or it did not read back; read `GET /api/v1/bouquets` and try again.
- `500 bouquet-not-saved`: the change is in the list the box runs, but its bouquet files may not hold it; do not send it again, read `GET /api/v1/bouquets`.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/bouquets`, `DELETE /api/v1/bouquets/{bouquet}`.

post.summary: asks the box to play one channel; refused with recording-holds-tuner while a recording holds the tuner the channel needs, with playback-running while the movie player plays a file unless stop_playback is set, and with box-in-standby in standby unless wake is set
post.description:
Switches live playback to the channel `channel_id` names, as choosing it on the remote control would. `202` means the box has queued the switch, not that it has happened: watch for the `zap` event on `GET /api/v1/events`, or read `GET /api/v1/channels/current`.

**Preconditions:** the box is not in standby, or `wake` is `true`. The movie player plays no file, or `stop_playback` is `true`. No running recording holds the tuner the channel needs.

**Refusals:**
- `404 no-such-channel`: no channel has that id. Take ids from `GET /api/v1/channels`.
- `409 recording-holds-tuner`: a recording occupies the tuner this channel needs. This is checked first, so neither `stop_playback` nor `wake` helps. Pick a channel the free tuner receives, or end the recording with `DELETE /api/v1/recordings/{id}`.
- `409 playback-running`: the movie player is playing a file, such as a finished recording, and `stop_playback` was not `true`. A web channel or the timeshift playing is not refused. Send again with `stop_playback: true` to end the playback and play the channel.
- `409 box-in-standby`: the box is in standby and `wake` was not `true`. Send again with `wake: true` to switch the box on and play the channel.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/mode`, `GET /api/v1/system/standby`, `POST /api/v1/system/standby`.

delete.summary: takes a bouquet away, with whatever it holds
delete.description:
Removes a bouquet together with the channel entries it holds. Every bouquet after it moves up 1 place, so the `id` numbers of `GET /api/v1/bouquets` change.

**Side effects:** the bouquet files are written, and every client sees a `bouquets-changed` event on `GET /api/v1/events`.

**Refusals:**
- `404 no-such-bouquet`: no bouquet has that name; read the names from `GET /api/v1/bouquets`.
- `409 name-shared`: more than one bouquet carries that name, so it names none of them; rename one of them on the box first.
- `409 bouquet-not-editable`: the box builds this bouquet itself (`editable` is false in `GET /api/v1/bouquets`) and makes it again, so a change to it would not last.
- `500 bouquet-not-changed`: the box did not take the change or it did not read back.
- `500 bouquet-not-saved`: the change is in the list the box runs, but its bouquet files may not hold it; do not send it again, read `GET /api/v1/bouquets`.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/bouquets`.

The box first takes the upload over: it copies it into a directory of its own and removes the upload, so what it checks is what it puts in place. The file holds no more than 16 MiB, the box's own XML reader takes it, and its root element is `zapit`, holding only `sat`, `cable` and `terrestrial` elements for `services` and `myservices`, each with its `name`, and only `Bouquet` elements for `bouquets` and `ubouquets`, which keeps a file sent as the wrong one of the 4 out. A setting marked a credential never carries its real default here; its default is always reported as an empty string.

Each item's `conditions` list states every comparison against another setting's current value that must hold before this setting is worth showing; an empty list means it is always shown.

`available` is false for a setting whose hardware this box lacks or cannot say it has; such a setting is not worth showing and refuses every write, while its value still reads. `locked` is true for a setting the box's parental lock fixes right now, which refuses every write too. Both are left out where they do not apply.

A member at its default is left out: `needs_restart`, `secret` and `listed` are false unless the item says otherwise. A list of choices that several items carry alike is stated once in the answer's `value_lists` object, and each such item names it in `values_from` instead of carrying `values`; read its entries the same way.

`section` narrows the list to one section, which keeps the answer small.

- `404 no-such-name`: no setting is declared under a section of that name. Take section ids from `GET /api/v1/settings/sections`.

patch.summary: writes settings of one section, answering the section as it reads now when every one of them landed and a result per key when they did not all agree
patch.description:
Writes one or more settings of a single section in one request. Every key is checked and, where valid, taken before any answer is built, so a read answers with it from then on and a value already landed is never rolled back by a later key failing. The box carries the values into its running settings and saves its configuration file on its own loop right after, and while a text input is open on the box it waits until that is closed.

When every key lands, the answer is `200` and is exactly the section's own `GET` answer: the section as it reads immediately afterward, which already reflects the new values, even though carrying them into the running program and telling the daemons that hold them happens afterward on the box's own loop. When more than one key was named and at least one of them failed, the answer is `207` with a `results` object naming each key and, for a failed one, its own status, `code` and `detail`; a request naming only one key that failed is instead answered as that one refusal, at its own status.

Two settings that are one fact in two parts carry `pair` and `pair_writes` in the schema. The id of a start channel sent alone is taken, and the box writes the name beside it from its channel list; that name is answered under its own key like a key that was sent. The name sent alone is refused, and a name sent with the id that its own row refuses is answered so while the id is taken as sent alone and the name of its channel is written beside it. The city and the location of the weather are refused when sent without each other, and sending a place other than the one the box holds empties `weather_postalcode`; a postal code sent with text in the same request is refused together with the city. Turning `epg_save` on turns `epg_read` on in the same write, answered under its own key, and `epg_read` sent off with it is refused together with it. A change of `lcd4l_display_type` brings `lcd4l_brightness` and `lcd4l_brightness_standby` down to what the new panel takes. Every value of a request is checked before any of them is taken, so a pair is not left half written by a value that could be refused beforehand; only a failure to store can still split one. A setting refused because another one was is answered `setting-condition-not-met`, and in a `207` its `depends_on` lists the settings that took it down.

A setting is also held to the `conditions` the schema states for it, the ones a screen of the box greys the setting out by: while they do not hold, it is refused `setting-condition-not-met`, and `depends_on` names the settings its conditions read that do not allow it. An entry of `values` that carries conditions of its own is refused the same way while they do not hold, with no `depends_on`. Both are judged on what the whole request leaves behind, so a setting and the one that allows it can be sent together in either order; in separate requests, the one that allows it goes first. A key refused for any reason counts as not sent, so what depends on it is refused too. A key that passes every check and then fails to be saved cannot be foreseen, so a setting depending on it may still land. A value equal to the one the box holds, or to the default of a key it never stored, passes the conditions of its setting, so a page may send a whole section back; for an entry with conditions of its own, the default passes as well. Such a value is answered as written and not written again. A credential is never taken as unchanged.

A setting marked `needs_restart` in the schema takes effect only the next time the box restarts, whatever this answers.

**Preconditions:** the section must be one the schema declares, and every key named must belong to that section.

**Side effects:** takes the value of every key that passes its checks, also in a `207` answer that names others as failed, and the box saves its configuration file when its own loop carries them. A settings-changed event follows on `GET /api/v1/events` once the box's own loop has saved a value that changed.

**Refusals:**
- `400 duplicate-parameter`: the same setting key is named twice in the body; neither value is written.
- `400 empty-credential`: a key marked a credential was sent an empty value; clear it with `POST /api/v1/settings/secret/clear` instead.
- `400 missing-parameter`: the body names no setting at all.
- `400 choices-unavailable`: the setting's values are the box's own and the box cannot say now what they are; only the value already stored and the default are taken then.
- `400 not-a-listed-value`: the value is not one the setting offers, among them the id of a radio channel sent for the television start channel or the other way round.
- `400 out-of-range`: a whole number value falls outside the min and max the schema states for that key, and is neither the value already stored nor the default, which stay writable after the box moved a range.
- `404 no-such-name`: the section itself is not one the schema declares. Take section ids from `GET /api/v1/settings/sections`.
- `404 no-such-channel`: the id sent alone for a start channel names no channel the box holds, so there is no name to write beside it.
- `404 no-such-setting`: a named key does not belong to this section, whether or not it exists elsewhere on the box.
- `409 setting-locked`: the schema marks the key `locked` (the parental lock); no write changes it.
- `409 setting-not-on-this-box`: the schema marks the key not `available`; this box does not have what it controls.
- `409 setting-condition-not-met`: the setting's `conditions` do not hold on what the request leaves behind, or the entry the value names is offered only while other settings allow it, or one half of a pair was sent without the other, together with a value that contradicts it, or beside a partner that was refused; `depends_on` and `detail` name the other settings, in a single refusal as in a `207`, except for an entry's own conditions.
- `500 channel-list-unavailable`: the id of a start channel was sent alone and the channel list could not be read to name it.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/settings/schema`, `GET /api/v1/settings/{section}`, `POST /api/v1/settings/secret/clear`.

post.summary: empties one credential, which is the one thing writing to it will not do
post.description:
Empties one credential setting, which is the only way to clear one: writing an empty value to it through `PATCH /api/v1/settings/{section}` is refused on purpose, so that a form redrawn from a read that answered nothing cannot wipe the value by accident. The answer is the same shape a section listing carries for one setting, and its `value` is empty, which is what the read of a credential always shows.

**Preconditions:** `key` must name a setting the schema marks `secret`, and it must be a string typed setting, which every credential in this program is. A credential whose text rule wants more than nothing, such as a pin of four digits, cannot be emptied.

**Side effects:** takes the empty value at once, so a read answers with it from then on; the box carries it into its running settings and saves its configuration file on its own loop, and while a text input is open on the box it waits until that is closed.

**Refusals:**
- `400 not-a-credential`: the setting is not a credential, or is a credential of a kind that has nothing to clear; this route is not a second way to write any other setting.
- `400 bad-string`: the credential's text rule does not take an empty value, such as a pin.

get.summary: what the box is and what it is running
get.description:
Reads what the box is and what it is currently running: the vendor, the model, the chipset, the firmware version, the kernel release, the hostname, its uptime, its memory and root filesystem usage, whether this build carries the API documentation, and the version of this interface itself. Every field is read fresh for each request but `image_version`, `os` and `support`, which are read once and kept for as long as the program runs.

**Refusals:**
- `500 box-unreadable`: the box could not be identified at all. This is a box fault, not a request problem; try again later.

get.summary: every process running on the box
get.description:
Lists every process running when the list is read, by process number: its parent, the user it runs as, its state, the memory it holds and has mapped, its name and the command line it was started with. Read out of the kernel's process table and not by starting a program, so asking changes nothing on the box. A process that ends while the list is read is left out.

**Refusals:**
- `501 processes-unreadable`: the box keeps no process list where this reads it.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/system/kernel-log`, `GET /api/v1/system/info`.

get.summary: the kernel's log, what dmesg prints
get.description:
Reads the kernel's log as it stands, oldest line first, each line with the level it was written at. Reading leaves the log as it is for every other reader.

**Refusals:**
- `501 kernel-log-unreadable`: the kernel does not hand its log to this program, which kernel.dmesg_restrict does for a program not running as root.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/system/processes`.

get.summary: whether the box is in standby
get.description:
Reads whether the box is in standby right now. The answer is read from the box's own mode, the same one `POST /api/v1/system/standby` changes, so it reflects a change made through the remote control or through the box's own menus just as well as one made through this interface. A box that is still starting up and has not settled on a mode yet answers false, because coming up is the opposite of standby.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/system/standby`.

post.summary: asks the box to go to standby or to come out of it
post.description:
Asks the box to go to standby or to come out of it, depending on `on`. `202` means the request has reached the box's own event loop, not that standby has changed yet: watch the `standby` event on `GET /api/v1/events`, or poll `GET /api/v1/system/standby`. Going to standby while already in it, or coming out of it while not in it, changes nothing and still answers `202`, which is why `on` must name the direction rather than this route toggling it.

**Side effects:** switching to standby stops live playback and the shift the box keeps of what it is showing; a recording or a timer already running is not stopped by it. While the box is in standby, `POST /api/v1/zap` and `POST /api/v1/mode` are refused with `409 box-in-standby` unless sent with `wake: true`, which switches the box on again as part of carrying out that request.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/system/standby`, `POST /api/v1/zap`, `POST /api/v1/mode`.

get.summary: what the running channel is being descrambled with
get.description:
Reads what the channel currently playing is being descrambled with: whether a softcam is answering for it right now, and whether a module seated in a common interface slot is being sent the channel. Both members are read afresh for each request and both can be false at once, which is a channel in the clear or one nothing can open. This says how the box is descrambling and never with what: no card number, no key and no name of a card server.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/daemons`, `GET /api/v1/channels/current`.

get.summary: the daemons this box can drive and which of them are running
get.description:
Lists every daemon this box can drive: the background services an image can carry, such as nfs, samba or crond. For each one, says whether a process of its name is currently in the process table and whether this box carries its systemd unit or init script at all, which may be false for a name every image knows but this build was not given. Softcams are not in this list.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/daemons/{name}/start`, `POST /api/v1/daemons/{name}/stop`, `POST /api/v1/daemons/{name}/restart`.

get.summary: how many times /control/ has been asked for each of its names, so retiring one can rest on what still calls it rather than on a guess, and no names at all where this build carries none of that surface
get.description:
Reads how many times the `/control/` surface has been asked for each of the names in its own table since this program started, plus any name it was asked for that table never had. It exists so that retiring a legacy name can rest on what still calls it rather than on a guess.

**Preconditions:** none, but on a build without the `/control/` surface at all this answers an empty list rather than refusing, so a page written against it works the same on both kinds of box.

post.summary: asks the box to restart itself
post.description:
Asks the box to restart itself: the Linux system reboots, not only this program. `202` means the request has reached the box's own event loop before this answer was sent, not that the box has restarted. If a recording is running, the box first shows a confirmation on its own screen; unless that is answered there, the reboot does not happen and this server keeps running, even though the answer already said `202`. When the reboot does go ahead, the connection this request arrived on is dropped and nothing further is answered on it. A client should expect the connection to close and should retry `GET /api/v1/system/info` after a pause to learn when the box is back.

**Side effects:** live playback and every daemon on the box stop; a recording that is allowed to proceed past the confirmation above is stopped as well.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/system/shutdown`, `POST /api/v1/system/restart`.

post.summary: asks the box to switch off
post.description:
Asks the box to switch off. `202` means the request has reached the box's own event loop, not that the box is off. While the box's stream server sends a channel to a client the request is dropped and nothing happens at all. While a recording is running, the box first shows a confirmation on its own screen; unless that is answered there, it does not switch off. With `shutdown_block_while_recording` on, the box instead goes into standby while a recording is running or a recording timer is still to come, and keeps retrying on its own until nothing is pending, rather than fully powering off straight away. Once it does power off, the connection this request arrived on is dropped and nothing further is answered on it. Unlike standby, shutdown is not reversed by a request to this interface: the box has to be switched on again at the box itself, by a timer that is due to wake it, or by whatever external power control it has.

**Side effects:** live playback and every daemon on the box stop once the box actually powers off.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/system/reboot`, `POST /api/v1/system/standby`.

get.description:
Packs the box's settings with its own backup.sh, the script the settings menu on the screen runs, and answers the archive as a file to keep (`application/gzip`, named `settings_<host>_<date>.tar.gz`): the files the box's tobackup.conf names, or its whole configuration directory where there is no such list. The archive holds the box's passwords and keys as its settings do, so it is for the box's own credential only.

**Refusals:**
- `500 backup-failed`: the box has no backup.sh, it failed, or it left no archive or one larger than 64 MiB.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/system/restore`.

post.summary: puts the settings of an uploaded archive back and restarts the box
post.description:
Puts back an archive uploaded to /tmp beforehand and restarts the box at once, as the settings menu does, so the program does not save its own settings over what was put back. A build for a PC that runs other things besides restarts only the program, started again in its own place without saving, and not the system (`--with-restore-restart`). `202` says the settings are back and the restart starts a few seconds later; the box, or the program, is then gone until it is up again. One restore runs at a time.

The box first takes the upload over: it copies it into a directory of its own under a name it chooses and removes the upload, so what it checks is what it puts back. Then every name in the archive is read from its headers. Each has to land in the configuration directory or on a path the box's tobackup.conf names: a directory, a file or a pattern. Names land below the box's /var/tuxbox where any of them begins with `config/`, and below `/` otherwise. An absolute name, one that climbs with `..`, one with a `.` or an empty part, one beginning with `.restore-`, a name with a control character, a link of either kind or a device in the archive, a link already on the box below where a name lands, a file where the box has a directory or the other way round, and an archive that holds one name as a file and as a directory or puts an entry below one of its files are refused, and so is an archive that cannot be read, one larger than 64 MiB, one whose headers say it unpacks to more than 256 MiB, or one of more than 20000 names.

The box unpacks the archive itself, with the same reading of its headers that checked it. From then on until the restart it saves no settings of its own, the saves under way finished first. Each file is written beside its place and takes its name only once every file is whole, with the permissions its entry carries, no set-id bits, and the owner the file had on the box where it had one; directories on the way, also a listed one the box does not have yet, are made where they are missing and not followed where they are links, and a directory entry sets its directory's permissions last.

**Preconditions:** the archive was uploaded to /tmp, as `PUT` and `PATCH /api/v1/storage/file` do in pieces for a file larger than one request.

**Refusals:**
- `400 bad-name`: `file` is not a plain name in /tmp ending in .tar.gz, .tgz or .tar.
- `404 no-such-name`: no file of that name was uploaded.
- `400 restore-refused`: the archive cannot be read or holds a name it may not; the detail names the first. Nothing was written.
- `409 restore-refused`: another restore is under way, or settings put back before wait for their restart.
- `500 restore-refused`: the box cannot restart itself, and nothing was put back; or it could not take the archive over or write a file of it, and its settings are as they were and it is not restarted; or, rarely, a file could not take its place after others had, and the settings are back in part and the box is not restarted; or the settings are back and the restart could not be started. The detail says which; in the last two the box saves no settings and has to be restarted by hand.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/system/backup`.

Asks the box to start its own application again without rebooting the Linux system underneath it. `202` means the request has reached the box's own event loop, not that the restart has happened. If a recording is running, the box refuses the restart with a message on its own screen, and this server keeps running, even though the answer already said `202`. When the restart does go ahead, the connection this request arrived on, and every other connection this server holds, is dropped as the program ends, and this server is unreachable until the new process has come up. A client should retry `GET /api/v1/system/info` after a pause.

**Side effects:** live playback stops and is set up again from scratch.

get.summary: how this server is set up: where it answers, who may tell it anything, and who reads from it without presenting anything
get.description:
Reads how this HTTP server itself is set up: the port and address it answers on, the account a caller signs in under, whether a password is set at all and whether it still waits to be replaced (one the boxes shipped with, or the first password the box set for itself), whether the pages ask for the login and of which callers not, how nhttpd serves the pages (threads, the override and hosted directories, files of unknown type), the networks that may read without presenting anything and the proxies whose forwarded address is believed, the file's `legacy_enabled` line, which nothing acts on (the surface under `/control/` is answered whatever it says), and whether a channel picture is served at all. This is a different file from `neutrino.conf`, which `/api/v1/settings` reads and writes.

**Related:** `PUT /api/v1/system/webserver`.

put.summary: sets this server up, naming only what is to change, and answers what the change means for the caller before the server is put on it
put.description:
Changes how this HTTP server itself is set up, naming only the members to change; a member left out keeps its stored value, and so does one sent as an empty string, except `no_login_prefix`, where an empty string is the value that exempts nobody. The file is written first, then this answer is sent, and only after it has gone out does the server, if anything that needs one changed, restart on the new file; a caller that moved the port or the bind address therefore still receives this answer on the connection it asked over.

The answer carries `webserver`, the configuration as the file now reads, and `caller`, what the change means for whoever asked: `address` is where to reach the server afterward, built from the name this request reached the box under and the new port, and empty when the request named no host; `port_moved` says whether the port changed; `password_changed` says whether the next sign in needs a different password, a session already open not being ended by it; `restarting` says whether anything changed enough to restart the server at all, since a request asking for what is already in effect changes nothing and restarts nothing.

**Side effects:** rewrites this server's own configuration file, and `nhttpd.conf` where `port`, `bind` or another member kept there differs from what that file says, that file being where the server answers and how nhttpd serves. When any member actually changed, the server is restarted on the new files once the answer has been sent, which drops every connection it is holding, this one included. Where nothing comes up on a new port or address, it goes back to the one it answered on before.

**Refusals:**
- `400 missing-parameter`: the body names nothing to change.
- `400 webserver-not-configured`: a value given could not be written, for instance a `bind` that is not an address literal of the first family, the only one this server listens on, a `no_login_prefix` that is not the start of an IPv4 address, a directory that is not an absolute path, or a configuration file itself could not be written; the detail names which.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/system/webserver`, `GET /api/v1/system/legacy-usage`.

get.summary: what the web interface keeps of its own beside the box's settings
get.description:
Reads the web interface's own settings file: the start page, the box's name and colour, the devices it wakes over the network, which extensions it shows and where, and what an extension keeps for itself, in `webui.conf`; a key nobody set is answered with the value the interface ships with. These are not the box's settings, which `/api/v1/settings` reads and writes. A key whose name says it holds a password, a PIN, a token or a key to a service is never answered; it is named in `withheld`.

**Related:** `PATCH /api/v1/webui/settings`.

patch.summary: writes keys of the web interface's own settings, answering the file as it then reads
patch.description:
Writes the keys the body names into the web interface's own settings file, in one write of the whole file, and answers it as `GET` does. A key left out keeps its value; an empty value takes the key out, which the pages read the same as a key that is not there. Every key and value is checked before anything is written, so a refused request leaves the file as it was.

**Refusals:**
- `400 bad-name`: a key is not a letter followed by up to 299 letters, digits, underscores, dots and dashes.
- `400 bad-string`: the body is not one flat object, or a value carries a control byte; `{=` or `=}`; one of `< > " ' `` ` `` or a backslash; or `#`, which the file reads as the start of a comment.
- `400 duplicate-parameter`: the body names one key twice.
- `400 missing-parameter`: the body names no key.
- `400 value-too-long`: a value is longer than 512 bytes.
- `409 too-many-settings`: the file would hold more than 256 keys.
- `500 setting-not-written`: the file could not be saved whole; the one there before is left in place.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/webui/settings`.

get.summary: the extensions of the web interface that are installed
get.description:
Lists the installed extensions of the web interface: each a directory under `/extensions/` with a `manifest.json`, which the pages read from there, and the shell scripts its manifest names that it holds. Which of them the pages show, and where, is in `GET /api/v1/webui/settings` (`ext_<dir>_enabled`, `ext_<dir>_slot`), and where those say nothing, in the manifest's `default` and `slot`.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/webui/extensions`, `DELETE /api/v1/webui/extensions/{dir}`.

post.summary: installs or replaces an extension from an archive uploaded to /tmp
post.description:
Installs the extension in an archive uploaded to /tmp beforehand, with `PUT` and `PATCH /api/v1/storage/file` for one larger than a request; an installed extension of that name is replaced, which is how one is updated. The box fetches nothing: a page that installs from an index loads the index and the archive itself and uploads both. An archive comes from a signed index, named in `index` with its `signature` and checked as `POST /api/v1/webui/extension-index` checks it, which has to offer the extension `dir` names with the archive's SHA-256; or, with `unsigned: true`, it is taken on the caller's word, which a page asks the user for. The box takes the upload over into a directory of its own and removes it, and reads the archive from its own headers: it has to hold exactly one directory, named with letters, digits, dashes and underscores, with a `manifest.json` in it, and only directories and regular files, no name that climbs or is absolute, no more than 16 MiB, 2000 names and 64 MiB unpacked. The manifest is a JSON object; the shell scripts it names under `scripts`, a list of names, are each `scripts/<name>.sh` in the archive. The extension is unpacked beside the installed ones, files readable by all, the scripts its manifest names executable and no other file, and only then does it take the place of one of its name; a file or a link in that place is replaced, never followed. Its scripts stay in its directory, where `POST /api/v1/webui/extensions/{dir}/scripts/{name}` runs them; copies an earlier install of it left beside the pages' own scripts go, where they are still as that install left them. An update names the extension it updates in `dir`, and an archive holding another one is refused. The upload goes in every case, and an index uploaded beside it with it.

**Refusals:**
- `400 bad-name`: `file` is not a plain name in /tmp ending in .tar.gz, .tgz or .tar, `dir` is no name an extension carries, or an install from an index names none.
- `404 no-such-name`: no archive of that name was uploaded.
- `400 extension-refused`: the archive comes neither from an index nor unsigned, the index does not hold to its signature or does not offer it, its SHA-256 differs, or it is not an extension this box takes or not the one `dir` names; the detail says why.
- `501 extension-refused`: an index was named and this image carries no key to check it with.
- `409 extension-refused`: another extension is being installed or removed.
- `500 extension-refused`: the disc refused; an installed extension of that name is as it was.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/webui/extensions`, `DELETE /api/v1/webui/extensions/{dir}`.

post.summary: runs one of an extension's scripts and answers what it wrote
post.description:
Runs a shell script of the installed extension `dir`, one its `manifest.json` names under `scripts`, from `scripts/<name>.sh` in the extension's own directory and nowhere else, waits for it to finish and answers what it wrote on its standard output as `output`. Each element of the body reaches the script as one argument, in order; no shell is involved, so a space or a quoting character reaches it as part of the argument. The settings page runs an extension's actions through this route.

**Preconditions:** the script finishes within 10 seconds and writes no more than 64 KiB; one that runs longer is stopped and refused. It runs as the account the server itself runs as, which can do anything on the box, so the route needs the `system` level.

**Refusals:**
- `400 bad-name`: no extension or script can carry that name.
- `400 bad-string`: the body is not one array of up to 32 strings, or an argument is longer than 1024 bytes; one longer than 4096 bytes is refused before that, as `400 value-too-long`.
- `400 leading-dash`: an argument begins with a dash, which the script would read as an option.
- `400 value-has-zero-byte`: an argument carries a zero byte.
- `404 no-such-name`: no extension of that name is installed.
- `404 script-missing`: its manifest names no script of that name, or the file is not there or cannot be run.
- `409 timeout`: the script ran longer than 10 seconds and was stopped.
- `500 exit-status`: the script failed, exiting with another status than 0.
- `500 output-too-large`: the script wrote more than 64 KiB.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/webui/extensions`.

**Refusals:**
- `400 bad-string`: `mac` is not six pairs of hexadecimal digits, separated by colons, dashes or nothing.
- `500 wake-not-sent`: the packet left on no network; the detail says why.

get.description: Lists every filesystem the kernel currently has mounted, read fresh from the kernel's own mount table for each request: where each one is mounted, what device or network share is mounted there, its filesystem type, and how large it is in total and free bytes. This is every mount on the box, not only the ones a recording or a file route may use; `total` and `free` are 0 for a mount point the kernel will not answer usage for. Network shares and FUSE filesystems are asked all at once and waited for about a second, so a share whose server went away does not hold the answer: it is in the list with `answered` false, and the same mount is not asked again while that question is still open. An automounter's own mount point is not asked.

get.description:

A name is inside the roots when it is one of them or lies below one; everything else on the box is out of reach of the file routes. Meant as the places a file manager offers to start from.

get.summary: what one directory inside the roots holds
get.description:
Lists the entries of one directory named by `path`, read fresh from the filesystem for each request: for every entry, its name, what kind of thing it is, and, where the filesystem could answer for it, its permission bits, link count, size, last written time, owner and group. The roots are the directories the box records to, where its movie browser looks, `/var` and `/tmp`, and the directories an image installs plugins into, rebuilt from the current recording path and movie browser settings before every request. The answer is not paged: it carries every entry the directory gave, in the order the directory gave them, which is not an order guaranteed to repeat.

**Preconditions:** `path` has to resolve inside one of the roots.

**Refusals:**
- `400 outside-roots`: `path` resolves outside every permitted directory.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/storage/mounts`, `GET /api/v1/storage/file`.

post.summary: makes one directory inside the roots
post.description:
Makes one directory at `path`. `201` means the directory exists on the filesystem by the time this answers, not merely that making it was asked for: this is a direct filesystem call and not a request handed to the box's own loop.

**Preconditions:** `path` has to resolve inside one of the roots, its parent directory has to exist already, and nothing may already be there under that name.

**Refusals:**
- `400 outside-roots`: `path` resolves outside every permitted directory.
- `409 name-taken`: something already exists under that name.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/storage/files`, `DELETE /api/v1/storage/path`.

post.summary: gives one name inside the roots another
post.description:
Renames `from` to `to` in one step on the same filesystem; what moves is the name itself, so a link is renamed as a link. `204` means the name has changed by the time this answers. A name already taken is left alone unless `overwrite` is `true`, and then only a plain file replaces a plain file, in one step, so a reader sees the old file or the new one and never neither.

**Preconditions:** both names have to lie inside the roots and on one filesystem, the directory that is to hold `to` has to exist, and neither name may be the web server's own access store. A root itself keeps its name.

**Refusals:**
- `400 access-store`: either name is the web server's own store of who may reach this box.
- `400 outside-roots`: either name resolves outside every permitted directory.
- `400 bad-name`: a name ends in `.` or `..` rather than in something to act on.
- `400 is-a-root`: `from` is one of the roots or holds one.
- `400 into-itself`: a directory was to move into something it holds.
- `400 cross-device`: the two names are on two filesystems; copy and remove instead.
- `404 no-such-name`: there is nothing at `from`.
- `404 no-such-parent`: the directory that is to hold `to` is not there.
- `409 name-taken`: something is already called `to` and `overwrite` was not `true`.
- `409 not-a-plain-file`: `to` is taken and one of the two is not a plain file.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/storage/files`, `PATCH /api/v1/storage/file`.

get.summary: the bytes of one file inside the roots
get.description:
Sends the bytes of one plain file named by `path`, straight out of the file on disk rather than copied through this process first, with a content type guessed from its name and a `Content-Disposition` header naming it for download. `200` carries the whole file; sending a `Range` header asks for part of it, which answers `206` with only that stretch, or `416` when the range does not fit inside the file. A name that is not there, or that is not a plain file (a directory, a device, a pipe), answers not found rather than saying which of those it is.

**Preconditions:** `path` has to resolve inside one of the roots and must not be the web server's own access store. A credential carried in the address itself rather than in a header is accepted here too; it reaches only the media roots (where the box records and where its movie browser looks), never the rest of the roots this route otherwise reaches, and is refused where it does not.

**Refusals:**
- `400 access-store`: `path` names the web server's own store of who may reach this box, which no file route reads, writes or removes.
- `400 outside-roots`: `path` resolves outside every permitted directory.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/storage/files`, `PUT /api/v1/storage/file`.

put.summary: puts one file inside the roots, as the bytes of the body
put.description:
Puts one file at `path`, with the whole request body as its bytes and nothing else: no form, no wrapper, no encoding. `201` means a new name was created; `204` means an existing name was replaced. The write is atomic: the bytes are written beside the final name first and put in its place in one step, so a transfer that breaks off leaves either the file that was there before or nothing at all, never a half written file. There is no ceiling of its own on the size beyond this server's general body ceiling, so this route suits configuration, lists and pictures rather than a recording or a firmware image.

**Preconditions:** `path` has to resolve inside one of the roots, its directory has to exist already, and it must not be the web server's own access store. Replacing an existing name needs `overwrite: true`; without it, an existing name is left alone. What is replaced has to already be a plain file, not a directory or anything else.

**Side effects:** writes or replaces the named file on the box's filesystem.

**Refusals:**
- `400 access-store`: `path` names the web server's own store of who may reach this box, which no file route reads, writes or removes.
- `400 outside-roots`: `path` resolves outside every permitted directory.
- `409 name-taken`: something is already there and `overwrite` was not `true`.
- `409 not-a-plain-file`: what is there is not a plain file, so nothing is put in its place.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/storage/file`, `DELETE /api/v1/storage/path`.

patch.summary: adds the next piece to the end of one file inside the roots
patch.description:
Adds the request body to the end of the plain file at `path`, which has to be exactly `offset` bytes long. For a file larger than one request may carry: the first piece is put with `PUT /api/v1/storage/file` under a name of its own, every further one is added here at the length the file has reached, and `POST /api/v1/storage/rename` gives it its real name at the end. A piece sent twice or one that went missing is refused, and the file is left as it was; its length says where to go on from. `204` means the bytes are in the file. `offset` is read as sixty four bits on every box, so a file goes past 4 GiB on one whose own numbers are thirty two bits wide.

**Preconditions:** `path` has to resolve inside one of the roots, name a plain file and not be the web server's own access store; `offset` has to be its length now.

**Side effects:** makes the named file longer by the body.

**Refusals:**
- `400 access-store`: `path` names the web server's own store of who may reach this box.
- `400 outside-roots`: `path` resolves outside every permitted directory.

- `404 no-such-parent`: the directory that would hold `path` is not there.
- `409 offset-mismatch`: the file is not `offset` bytes long; a piece went missing or came twice.
- `409 not-a-plain-file`: what is at `path` is not a plain file.

**Related:** `PUT /api/v1/storage/file`, `POST /api/v1/storage/rename`.

post.summary: mounts one slot's share
post.description:
Mounts the slot's share on its local directory, which is made where it is missing, as the screen at the box does. Waits for the mount, up to a few seconds; the answer is all 8 slots as they read afterwards.

**Refusals:**
- `501 command-not-sent`: this box keeps no network shares of its own.
- `409 share-not-configured`: the slot names no server or no remote directory.
- `409 mount-point-busy`: something is mounted on the local directory already, this share among it.
- `501 filesystem-unsupported`: this box cannot mount a share of that kind, or the slot is of the userspace FTP filesystem, which is mounted at the box.
- `500 timeout`: the server did not answer in time.
- `500 mount-failed`: the mount failed otherwise; the box's log says why.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/storage/shares/{slot}/unmount`, `POST /api/v1/storage/shares/mount`.

- `500 unmount-failed`: the unmount failed; something on the box may still be using it.

get.summary: the box's own events as they happen
get.description:
Opens a Server-Sent Events stream (`text/event-stream`) on which the box announces changes as they happen, whoever caused them: this API, the remote control or a timer. The connection stays open; read it with `EventSource` or any SSE client. The stream begins with a `retry:` line of 10 to 19 seconds, the time a client waits before it reconnects, and carries a comment line (`:`) as a heartbeat when nothing happens.

Each event is an `event:` line with its name and a `data:` line with a JSON object `{"channel_id": hex string, "value": integer, "text": string}`. Events say what changed, not everything about it: reread the matching route.

| event | meaning | carries |
|---|---|---|
| `zap` | the box switched channel | `channel_id`: the new channel |
| `mode` | the box changed mode | `value`: 1 TV, 2 radio, 4 standby, other values for the player modes |
| `standby` | standby was entered or left | `value`: 1 in standby, 0 awake |
| `volume` | the volume changed | `value`: 0 to 100 |
| `mute` | sound was muted or unmuted | `value`: 1 muted, 0 sound on |
| `record-start` | a recording began | `channel_id`, `value`: the recording id of `GET /api/v1/recordings` |
| `record-stop` | a recording ended | `channel_id`, `value`: the recording id |
| `timer-changed` | the timer list changed | nothing; reread `GET /api/v1/timers` |
| `epg-updated` | the guide got now and next for a channel | `channel_id`: only its lower 48 bits; at most 1 per 500 milliseconds, others in between are dropped |
| `bouquets-changed` | the bouquet list changed | nothing; reread `GET /api/v1/bouquets` |
| `settings-changed` | settings were written | nothing; reread `GET /api/v1/settings/{section}` |
| `playback` | the movie player started, stopped, paused, resumed, jumped or changed speed | `text`: the state (`playing`, `paused`, `forward`, `rewind` or `stopped`), the source as `GET /api/v1/playback` names it and, for a recording, its archive id, separated by spaces; `value`: the position in seconds; `channel_id`: the channel of a recording or a timeshift, else 0 |

**Refusals:**
- `503 too-many-streams`: the server already carries as many event streams as it is set to (16 by default); close another one or try later.

**Related:** every route whose description names an event.

post.summary: opens a session for a name and a password, and says what that session carries and is worth
post.description:
Checks the name and password against the single account this box is configured with and, when they match, opens a session for it. The answer carries the session state: `authenticated`, `level`, `user`, the second token `csrf` to send back in the header `csrf_header` names on every request that changes something, and `expires_in` in seconds. The session itself travels in a `Set-Cookie` header (`HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, no expiry attribute, so the browser forgets it when it closes). A session runs out after the configured lifetime without a request; every request it carries starts that lifetime again, up to 30 days after the login.

**Preconditions:** a username and a password hash must be configured on the box; a box with neither configured never matches whatever is sent, so login always fails.

**Side effects:** opens an entry in the in-memory session table and sets the session cookie. Nothing is written to disk. Wrong attempts from the same address are delayed: the first 2 cost nothing extra, every one after that doubles the wait up to a ceiling of 60 seconds, and the record is forgotten after 10 minutes without another attempt from that address. At most 4 logins are checked at once across every address; a 5th caller arriving at the same moment is asked to retry rather than queued.

**Refusals:**
- `401 not-permitted`: the name and the password do not go together. An unknown name and the right name with the wrong password are answered the same way and cost the same time to check, so a caller cannot use the delay to learn which it was.
- `429 too-many-attempts`: either this address is still inside its backoff delay, or 4 logins are already being checked at once; the `Retry-After` header carries how many seconds to wait before trying again.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/session`, `POST /api/v1/logout`.

user.description: the account name, which must match the single username this box is configured with

password.description: the password for that account, checked against the stored hash and never echoed back

get.summary: says what the request asking carries: whether it holds a session, what it was granted, and the second token to send back with what it changes
get.description:
Reads the credentials the request itself carries (the session cookie, a bearer token, or a token in the query where a route allows one) and answers the same session-state document the login answer carries: whether the caller is authenticated, the access level granted to this request, the user name, the second token `csrf` with the header name `csrf_header` it travels in, and how many seconds the session has left in `expires_in`. A request holding no session, or one that has run out, is answered the same way: `authenticated` false, empty `user` and `csrf`, `expires_in` 0, and as `level` what the request is granted without a session: the level of a bearer token it carries, `read` from a network allowed to read without signing in, `public` otherwise.

This route is open to every caller, including one presenting nothing, so that a page which has lost its session, for instance after a reload, can find that out without the gate refusing the request for carrying no second token. A `GET` is a safe method, so no second token is needed here even though the cookie is read.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/login`, `POST /api/v1/logout`.

post.summary: closes the session this request arrived with
post.description:
Closes the session named by the request's own cookie, and tells the browser to forget that cookie by sending it back with `Max-Age=0`. Whether a session actually existed is not reported to a request that may write: one carrying a bearer token and no session is answered the same `204` as one that really closed something.

**Preconditions:** the request needs write access, which a live session or a bearer token of the `write` or `system` level gives; a cookie whose session has run out gives none, and such a request is refused with `403` like any other. A request that writes with its session cookie must also carry the second token in the header this server names (`X-CSRF-Token` by default); one authenticated by a bearer token does not.

**Side effects:** removes the session's entry from the in-memory session table and clears the cookie in the browser. A scoped token minted through that session ends with it.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/session`, `POST /api/v1/login`.

put.summary: replaces the account's password with one of the owner's own
put.description:
Sets the password of the single account this box has. The password in effect is asked for again in `current`; a wrong one is counted against the address like a wrong login. The new password has at least 8 characters, holds no control characters, is none of the passwords these boxes have shipped with and is not the one it replaces. It is in effect for every login when this answers; sessions already open stay open, the one asking among them.

While the box still opens to a password it shipped with, or to the first password it set for itself and showed on its screen, this is the route a caller signed in with it is to use: every route but this one, `POST /api/v1/login`, `GET /api/v1/session` and `POST /api/v1/logout` refuses it with `403 password-change-required`, which `GET /api/v1/session` announces as `password_change_required`. The old `/control/` routes keep answering the box's login as they always did.

**Side effects:** the stored form of the password is written to nhttpd-access.conf; the password itself is kept nowhere.

**Refusals:**
- `400 bad-string`: the new password is too short, holds a control character, is one these boxes have shipped with, or is the one it replaces; the detail says which.
- `403 not-permitted`: `current` is not the password in effect.
- `429 too-many-attempts`: wrong passwords were sent from this address too often, or too many are being checked at once; `Retry-After` says how long to wait.
- `500 webserver-not-configured`: the box could not write the new password; the old one stays in effect.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/login`, `GET /api/v1/session`.

post.summary: draws a short lived token that reaches the media this box holds and nothing else, for a player that can carry a credential only in the address
post.description:
Mints a token scoped to the media this box holds, such as recordings, and answers it together with its scope and lifetime in seconds, for a player that can only carry a credential in the address and not in a header or a cookie. Append it as `?token=...` to `GET /api/v1/storage/file`, where it reaches only files under the media directories, or to the archive file and playlist routes.

The scope is always `media` and cannot be chosen. On every other route the token is not a credential at all, in the query or as a bearer header, so a leaked address exposes the media and nothing more.

**Preconditions:** the caller must already be granted the system level, by a session or by a bearer token minted at that level, since this route requires it.

**Side effects:** records the token's hash and expiry in memory only; nothing is written to disk, so the token stops working the moment the box restarts. It lives 6 hours from the moment it is drawn, and a token drawn through a session ends earlier when that session ends, by logging out or by running out.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/login`, `GET /api/v1/storage/file`, `GET /api/v1/recordings/archive/{id}/file`, `GET /api/v1/recordings/archive/{id}/playlist.m3u`.

get.summary: every timer the box holds
get.description:
Lists every timer the timer daemon holds, with what each one does and when. Not paged: a box holds tens of timers, not thousands. A timer leaves the list once it has run for the last time; a repeating one is rescheduled and stays.

Use the `id` of an entry to change it with `PATCH /api/v1/timers/{id}` or remove it with `DELETE /api/v1/timers/{id}`.

**Refusals:**
- `timer-list-unavailable` (a 5xx status): the timer daemon could not be read; try again later.

**Related:** `POST /api/v1/timers`, the `timer-changed` event on `GET /api/v1/events`.

post.summary: makes a timer and answers where it can be reached
post.description:
Makes a timer in the box's timer daemon, the same daemon the box's own timer list shows. `kind` decides what it does and which other members matter (see the list under `kind`); `start` is always required. The answer is `201` with the new timer's decimal `id` and a `Location` header `/api/v1/timers/{id}`.

For a recording of a programme from the guide, send `kind` `record`, the `channel_id`, the event's `start` and `start + duration` as `stop`, and optionally `epg_id`, `epg_start` and `title` from `GET /api/v1/epg/event`. `recording_safety` and `auto_adjust` are off unless sent, so the timer keeps exactly the times given.

For a recording that starts at once, send `kind` `immediate-record`. It begins at the box's own time, so a caller whose clock is behind or stale is not refused: a `stop` sent with `epg_start` stays as sent while it lies ahead, and any other `stop` keeps its distance from `start`.

**Preconditions:** none on the box state: a timer can be made in standby, and a `record` or `zapto` timer wakes the box from deep standby before it is due.

**Side effects:** the daemon stores the timer in its file and every client sees a `timer-changed` event on `GET /api/v1/events`.

**Refusals:**
- `400 timer-without-channel`: `zapto`, `record` or `immediate-record` without `channel_id`.
- `400 recording-without-duration`: a recording whose `stop` is not after `start`.
- `400 no-such-parameter`: a `stop` other than `0` for a kind that does not record.
- `400 not-a-listed-value`: a `repeat` value outside the table under `repeat`.
- `400 timer-in-the-past`: a timer that runs once (`repeat` 0) with a `start` more than 120 seconds before the box's current time, except `immediate-record`. Send a later `start`.
- `409 timer-exists`: the daemon already holds a timer like this one; find it with `GET /api/v1/timers`.
- `timer-not-created`, `clock-unavailable`: the daemon declined or the box could not read its clock; try again.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/timers`, `PATCH /api/v1/timers/{id}`, `DELETE /api/v1/timers/{id}`, `GET /api/v1/epg/event`.

kind.description:
what the timer does when it fires; the kind decides which other members it reads

- `shutdown`: switches the box off at `start`
- `zapto`: switches to `channel_id` at `start`, waking the box from deep standby for it; needs `channel_id`
- `standby`: at `start` puts the box into standby when `standby_on` is `true`, and brings it out of standby when it is `false`
- `record`: records `channel_id` from `start` to `stop`, waking the box from deep standby for it; needs `channel_id` and a `stop` after `start`
- `remind`: shows `title` on the screen at `start`
- `sleeptimer`: at `start` switches the box off or puts it into standby, whichever the box's own shutdown setting chooses
- `exec-plugin`: starts the plugin named in `title` at `start`
- `immediate-record`: a recording of `channel_id` that begins at once, at the box's own time, whatever `start` says; with `epg_start` and a `stop` still ahead on the box's clock, `stop` is kept as the end, otherwise `stop - start` is the length counted from the box's now; it is filed, and read back, as `record`

x-enum-descriptions.zapto: switches to `channel_id` at `start`, waking the box from deep standby for it; needs `channel_id`
x-enum-descriptions.standby: at `start` puts the box into standby when `standby_on` is `true`, and brings it out of standby when it is `false`
x-enum-descriptions.record: records `channel_id` from `start` to `stop`, waking the box from deep standby for it; needs `channel_id` and a `stop` after `start`
x-enum-descriptions.sleeptimer: at `start` switches the box off or puts it into standby, whichever the box's own shutdown setting chooses
x-enum-descriptions.exec-plugin: starts the plugin named in `title` at `start`
x-enum-descriptions.immediate-record: a recording of `channel_id` that begins at once, at the box's own time, whatever `start` says; with `epg_start` and a `stop` still ahead on the box's clock, `stop` is kept as the end, otherwise `stop - start` is the length counted from the box's now; it is filed, and read back, as `record`

channel_id.description: the channel to switch to or record, hexadecimal as `GET /api/v1/channels` answers it; required for `zapto`, `record` and `immediate-record`, ignored by the other kinds

start.description: when the timer fires, Unix time in seconds; for a timer that runs once it may lie at most 120 seconds before the box's current time and then fires at once, while a repeating timer may start further in the past and also fires at once; an `immediate-record` begins at the box's current time and uses `start` only to measure its length

stop.description: when a recording ends, Unix time in seconds, after `start`; any value but `0` is refused for the kinds that do not record

title.description: the programme title stored with a `record` or `immediate-record` timer, the text a `remind` timer shows, or the name of the plugin an `exec-plugin` timer starts; ignored by the other kinds, and cut to what the daemon stores

repeat.description:
how the timer repeats, as a number:

| value | repeats |
|---|---|
| 0 | never, it runs once (the default) |
| 1 | daily |
| 2 | weekly |
| 3 | every 2 weeks |
| 4 | every 4 weeks |
| 5 | monthly |
| 256 + day bits | on the chosen weekdays |

For weekdays, add 256 and the bit of every day: Monday 512, Tuesday 1024, Wednesday 2048, Thursday 4096, Friday 8192, Saturday 16384, Sunday 32768. At least 1 day is needed, so Monday to Friday is 256 + 512 + 1024 + 2048 + 4096 + 8192 = 16128 and every day is 65280. Any other value is refused with `400 not-a-listed-value`.

repeat_count.description: how many times a repeating timer runs, and `0` (the default) for without end

announce.description: when the box announces the timer, Unix time in seconds; left out, `0` or less, or later than `start`, it becomes 60 seconds before `start`, or 180 seconds before it for `record`; an `immediate-record` timer has none. A box in deep standby wakes at least 3 minutes before this for a timer that wakes it

epg_id.description: the guide event the timer is made from, hexadecimal as `GET /api/v1/epg` answers it, for `record` and `zapto`; with `auto_adjust` the box follows the programme the guide has in the middle of the recording

epg_start.description: when that guide event begins, Unix time in seconds, sent together with `epg_id`

standby_on.description: for a `standby` timer only: `true` puts the box into standby at `start`, `false` (the default) brings it out of standby

recording_dir.description: the directory a `record` timer writes to, as a path on the box; empty or left out for the box's own recording directory

recording_safety.description: whether the box widens a recording by the margins it is set to, starting it earlier and stopping it later; `false` when left out, so the timer keeps exactly the `start` and `stop` sent

auto_adjust.description: whether the box moves a recording onto the guide's own times for the programme the guide has in the middle of the recording, which it does only where the box is set up for it; `false` when left out

patch.summary: changes what a timer the daemon holds may be changed about
patch.description:
Changes the times and the repetition of a timer the daemon holds and answers the timer as the daemon reads it afterwards. Send only the members to change: everything left out keeps its value. Only `start`, `stop`, `repeat`, `repeat_count` and `announce` can be changed; to change the kind, the channel, the title or the standby flag, remove the timer with `DELETE /api/v1/timers/{id}` and make a new one with `POST /api/v1/timers`.

Moving `start` moves an announcement that was set by the same amount, unless `announce` is sent too, which a running recording ignores.

**Preconditions:** a recording that runs once and has already begun can only have its `stop` changed, and its new `stop` must lie after now.

**Side effects:** the daemon stores the change and every client sees a `timer-changed` event on `GET /api/v1/events`.

**Refusals:**
- `404 no-such-timer`: the daemon holds no timer with that id; read the ids again from `GET /api/v1/timers`.
- `409 recording-running`: a `start` other than the current one for a recording that runs once and has begun.
- `400 timer-in-the-past`: a timer that runs once moved more than 120 seconds before the box's current time, or a running recording given a `stop` before now.
- `400 recording-without-duration`: a recording whose `stop` would not lie after its `start`.
- `400 no-such-parameter`: a `stop` other than `0` for a timer that does not record.
- `400 not-a-listed-value`: a `repeat` outside the table under `repeat`, including a timer that already carries such a value and is changed without sending a new `repeat`.
- `timer-not-changed`: the daemon did not take the change; read the timer again.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/timers`, `DELETE /api/v1/timers/{id}`.

- `timer-not-removed` (a 5xx status): the daemon did not take the removal; try again.

get.summary: how loud the box is and whether the sound is off
get.description:
Reads the current volume and the mute flag together, both taken at the same moment. The volume is a percentage from 0 to 100 and is independent of mute: muting does not change it, so turning the sound back on restores the level it had before.

**Refusals:**
- `500 mute-unavailable`: the mute state could not be read from the box.

put.summary: asks the box to change the volume
put.description:
Sets the volume to `percent`, a value from 0 to 100. `202` means the box has queued the change, not that it has been applied: watch for the `volume` event on `GET /api/v1/events`, or read `GET /api/v1/osd/volume` again. The level is carried to the box in a single byte, which is why it is bounded to 0 to 100 both here and once more before it is applied. On a muted box, a level above 0 also turns mute off; a level of 0 leaves it muted.

**Related:** `GET /api/v1/osd/volume`, `PUT /api/v1/osd/mute`.

- `404 no-such-channel`: no channel has that id.

- `409 no-free-tuner`: no tuner is free for this channel without changing what the box shows - the picture, a picture in picture, a recording and other streams keep theirs; a channel the box shows can be streamed from the picture's own tuner, a channel streamed already is shared, and a channel being recorded is refused, as on the streaming port. Where switching the TV picture to the channel would free the picture's tuner, the setting `streaming_switch_picture` decides: switched on, as it is by default, the stream is answered and the box switches the picture as it starts (only while it shows live television or radio of the channel's kind and records nothing); switched off, the refusal carries `depends_on: ["streaming_switch_picture"]`, and a HEAD as well as a GET the header `X-Depends-On: streaming_switch_picture`, so a client can offer that setting. The picture is never switched to or away from a channel the box would ask the PIN for, and such a refusal carries no `depends_on`; nor is it switched while the box holds it back for the PIN.
- `503 too-many-conversions`: the box is already converting as many streams as it will, at most 2 at once; retry after the time named in the `Retry-After` header.
- `503 upstream-unreachable`: the box could not say within two seconds whether a tuner is free, or the converter ended or stayed silent for 15 seconds before it sent anything, so the channel could not be read; a HEAD asked afterwards says what is in the way now.
- `500 no-supervision`: the box's program discards what its children exit with at the moment, so it cannot run a converter it could stop again.

Lists the finished recordings in the media library and the folders directly below each of its directories, newest first, 15 to a page unless `limit` says otherwise. The library is the directories the box's movie browser is set to look in: the record directory and its own list, each only while switched on there. A directory on a share that does not answer within two seconds is left out of this answer and of `sources`. One that answered but is still being read the first time is left out too and sets `partial`; ask again shortly. Every directory is read again once its last reading is 30 seconds old and when a recording ends or is removed, and the answer waits up to two seconds for that; a reading that takes longer is answered with what the one before it found. A file added by other means can take up to 30 seconds to appear. `source` says where each recording lies and narrows the list to one directory; a recording two directories hold counts for the first of them unless `source` names the other. A recording is a transport stream the box wrote with its metadata file beside it; title, channel and length come from that file, `start` is reckoned from when the stream was last written and that length. `title` narrows the list to titles holding those words. `sort` orders the matching recordings by `title`, `start`, `channel`, `duration` or `size` before the page is cut; `order` left out is `desc` for `start`, `duration` and `size` and `asc` for `title` and `channel`.
